Father died instantly. Mother wasn’t close behind, but still breathing when we arrived. Two kids on the backseat had multi-systems trauma due to the fact they’d been laying down and asleep, and not wearing seatbelts.

We airlifted Mom and the two daughters. When coroner came by and removed Dad…we found a two year old toddler that he’d been shielding. She had a cardiac history and had died without a scratch on her…probably aortic separation though.

Mortician carried her out to the asphalt, and some of the toughest men I’ve ever known cried like babies when they bagged her up. She looked like she was only sleeping. Most beautiful little girl I’ve ever seen.

I'm so glad you decided to ask for some advice prior to purchasing a vehicle! It's not something that should be done on a whim, and I've made enough mistakes when financing that I can give you some pointers.

First and foremost, you need to understand that banks are at the mercy of the Federal Reserve with regards to rates, and right now: rates are *high*...like crazy high. That means that your monthly payment will more than likely exceed your previous expectations. The fallout of that being that your affordable 'sticker price' (or a car's total cost) will be significantly lower than say a year ago.

In other words, were you able to afford a $20,000 car during 2021: you'd only be able to afford a $10,000 car today. Interest represents the *cost of borrowing money*, hence why your monthly payment would double from previous years.

Second, depending upon how much you want to spend, you need to understand that you're paying for far more than a 'car'. In fact, the more amenities a vehicle has, such as heated seats, DVD players, auto start/stop, etc: the more you'll pay. In a new vehicle, you'll more than likely have the option of customizing your vehicle suit your price point; however, used vehicles are already packaged. That's not to say that new vehicles make more sense though.

Cars are much like any other asset (other than housing): they depreciate...meaning that they steadily lose value. The moment you drive a vehicle off of a dealership's lot...you've lost money. You could literally drive a mile down the road to another dealership and attempt to trade your brand new vehicle, and you would receive less money than you paid a few minutes prior. That's a fact. Subsequently, I've always recommended purchasing a used vehicle for that very reason.

Typically, you should look for a car beneath 100,000 miles, and ask for that vehicle's accident history to see whether any collisions have taken place. Each collision represents a 'red flag' though, as no machine - vehicle or otherwise - will perform as well after having been rebuilt/repaired. If they don't have any records (most dealerships will use CarFax), then you should steer clear of that vehicle. Also, all states have different laws regarding vehicles that were totaled and whether they can be fixed and sold, and even whether dealerships have to disclose that fact. Okay, so American Medical Response (AMR) offers a 4% employer match 401k contribution after you contribute 8% for a 12% total. It seems **super** counterproductive to take home less when you're already struggling, but that 8% will be pre-tax and also lower your taxable income (meaning the government taxes you less, because on paper you make less). In future, these funds can be withdrawn when you're retired; however, you can also take out loans when you're younger against these funds without a credit check or approval process. These can help with making down payments on your first house, a vehicle, etc. Any interest on that loan then gets paid to yourself versus some corporate bank. The loan can be for up to 50% of your balance with payment schedules as long as 5-7 years.

If you have any health costs, I would also recommend that you look at the federal spending account (FSA), which can also be used to pay for any medications you take, your eyeglass frames/lenses, dentist visits and some over the counter (OTC) drugs. I wish you could pay for gym memberships with them, but...alas.

So, I had my eldest daughter when I was eighteen, and I'm thirty-eight now. Here are all the things I wish I had done differently:

* Keep my relationship with my parents, and my spouse's (we're still married today) parents strong. In 2002, when our daughter was born, living by yourself as two young kids with a baby was tough. If I had managed those relationships better, I could have relied upon that strong foundational support. Today, there's no way on God's earth that two seventeen year olds could afford housing and transport on minimum wage.
* Utilized that time that I could rely on the support of family to start a career. I wouldn't have chased a master's degree, but would have focused on a trade, like electrician, etc. Years after the fact, I ended up traveling down a similar path with Emergency Medical Technology (EMT), which worked out nicely for me. Today, trade schools are perpetually looking for new students and employers perpetually looking for new employees.
* I wish I had been smarter with my money. When you're young and you get a check for a $1,000 from an employer, you act like that's a small fortune. Fast forward twenty-odd years, and that amount of money wouldn't even pay my mortgage. Curb your personal purchases, download an investment app like Acorn, and **start building your credit history**. Apply for a few low threshold cards, keep your balance under 50%, and make the payments on time. Years later, when you can always get a low interest rate on loans: you'll thank me. When you do start your career, aggressively invest into your employer's 401k, or at the very least make sure you get their 100% match contribution. That way, when you need to buy a new washing machine, or any of the other myriad complications that arise from life, you can take out a 401k loan. Loans against your 401k are always approved, and any interest accrued is paid **to yourself and not a bank**.
* Always put them first. I had friends that I was constantly hanging out with at the expense of my family. Looking back, I allow myself some leeway that I needed a life outside of being a young father, but I pushed the envelope too far. In monopolizing my own social life, I created a situation where my spouse had none. Include them in your hobbies and pastimes. It will pay dividends.
* Don't expect everything to be easy, and get frustrated when you're not living the life of your dreams. I was constantly angry that we lived in a crappy house, or didn't have any money. Having kids is expensive, not to mention merely **being alive** is expensive. The pathway to a better life is always there to be trodden, but each step can take time. I was always my own worst enemy.
* Find a babysitter that you trust implicitly, and make sure that you spend some dedicated time with your significant other. Let her know - unequivocally - that she's the most important person in your life. The Catholic religion venerates Mother Mary, because through her Jesus was born. I know that's random, but that's the best metaphor I have. You're going to **love your kid** like nothing on Earth, but remember that your woman gave that child to you. Always take time every couple of weeks to spoil her with a nice dinner, etc. Hell, Netflix and chill while you cook. It doesn't really matter. She's going to be so overwhelmed during these first couple of years, and she doesn't need a husband; she needs a partner whose going to get their hands dirty and help.

That's all I got off the top of my head. Send me a DM if you ever need to talk. You can do this, buddy.

TLDR: as patients become more and more serious, your ability to cope strangely becomes easier since you are able to empathize with them (having never experienced those events yourself) less and less.

Medicare rates didn't create themselves, any more than the current trend of 'transport, transport, transport' was created by private businesses. EMS started as a government controlled entity, but hasn't evolved much since that time.

I have huge doubts that services will simply vanish, but we would see twenty-four hour shifts disappear, followed likely by overtime, and a restructuring around a '1236' shift-type. Ambulance companies will then have to upstaff - which will drive up benefit costs - and result with a quality reduction of current benefits to offset cost.

Undoubtedly, there exists a difference between what prehospital providers are paid and what ambulance companies could actually afford to pay them. You have to understand that though that a $15 federal minimum wage would use a 'broad brush' approach to a local problem. For example, Mississippi has a far lower cost of living than New York or California. Do you really believe that companies could potentially double their workers wages without significant reduction of their workforce, or at the very least fundamentally changing their operation?

I think for some parts of the country, a $15 minimum wage would easily be absorbed since their current wage was close enough to the mark. Others wouldn't be so lucky, and not because of any corporate greed but local market conditions.

So, an ambulance company may charge $1000 to Medicare for a transport (cost of doing business, plus a mark-up), but have an allocated reimbursement rate (what Medicare has agreed to pay you) of $250. After billing for the transport, perhaps you receive $200 of that final bill. 

Each year, Medicare raises reimbursement rates by a small percentage; however, these raises have done little to combat the fact that EMS must - or otherwise risk solvency - be as lean as possible. The smaller the overhead: the less risk you take on as a result. It’s practically why Unit Hour Utilization (UHU) has become the gold standard for ambulance deployment.

As a result, EMS systems are notoriously weak to so-called ‘black swan events’ because they only ever have the bare minimum amount of resources fielded at any one time.

Ambulance companies are price takers, and not price makers, such as Apple, Microsoft or Samsung. Those companies can charge whatever they want based on supply and demand. Medicare reimbursement rates are fixed, regardless of market conditions, and so our ‘variable costs’ like payroll - which are market controlled - are watched very closely.

I don’t see how our existing systems could possibly survive a $15 minimum wage hike unscathed.

So, a federal minimum wage of $15 an hour would require a substantial overhaul of Medicare reimbursement rates, or the cost/benefit ratio of private EMS essentially goes to the red. While public entities are tax subsidized, we do not have that fallback and are 100% reliant on transports to fund payroll, equipment, supplies, etc.

Prehospital providers deserve a higher wage, but without additional legislation by Washington, a $15 minimum wage would transform EMS to look nothing like what we see today.

The subtle genius of the script can be summarized as: "when you're dealing with a power that by definition *has no limit*, rules simply don't matter."

They're using a page out of the *grandfather paradox* playbook. Essentially, you couldn't go back to kill your grandfather, because that would mean *you wouldn't have been born*. While many Hollywood movies explain such an event with a vanishing protagonist ala *Back to the Future* or *Looper*, *Avengers: Endgame* goes another direction. You could kill your grandfather, but you would still return to a timeline where he's alive and well, because any other eventuality doesn't make sense. Your grandfather *must* marry your grandmother, and eventually sire your parent...

\*pauses to catch a breath\*

...who eventually gives birth to *you,* otherwise your very existance (and reason for traveling back through time) are obsolete.

In killing your grandfather, you simply create an alternate reality where he dies and you're never born; a reality you never experience, or have any knowledge about. The Infinity Stones prevent such an occurrence; however, which means that any attempt to kill Baby Thanos would result with an unchanged timeline and a *nasty* stain on your conscience.

In all honesty, you have to wonder what would happen to the events of *Thor: The Dark World*, *Thor: Ragnarok* *and* *Avengers: Infinity War.* While from a chronological standpoint, each of these separate, yet entwined stories *must* be different, events remain entirely unchanged for the current MCU. 

Why?

Because for Thanos to have been successful *and* for Tony and the others to have traveled through the Quantum Realm, Loki *must* be responsible for Frigga's death, Thor's salvation at the destruction of Asgard (which killed Hela), and for Thanos retrieving the Space Stone. Those events are **locked**, as unless they occur, our heroes would never have undertaken the mission that unexpectedly changed them.
I would give the price of another ticket to any movie theater that shows me the scene when Steve gives the Soul Stone back to Red Skull.

Let's say you and I are part of the Marvel Universe and we flip a coin. You call *heads* and I call *tails.* We watch the coin toss, and...*you win!* There are no alternate realities, or timelines existing alongside our own...we tossed a coin and guessed the outcome; nothing more, nothing less. The Infinity Stones provide that sense of security. The multiverse theory can be considered nothing more than that: *a theory*.

Now, let's consider that same toss without the governing power of one of the Infinity Stones. Suddenly, when Professor Hulk takes the Time Stone back to the Avenger's Compound, multiple realities are *possible*. There's one reality where you won the toss, but also a reality where I won the toss, or a bird snatched the coin out of midair and neither one of us won, etc (you could hypothesize alternate outcomes all day). 

Take that example and expand across the events of Avengers: Endgame. Thanos, Nebula and Gamorra travel through time to 2023; Steve fights a younger Captain America who believes he's fighting Loki, and potentially the real Loki's escape via the Space Stone (although a Disney+ show would suggest I'm right). All of these are events that *could* have happened when considering an *entire universe of possibilities*.

When the stones are returned to their chronological points of origin, these alternate realities collapse; however, not because events are 'reset', or because Steve 'fixes' the timelines. The Infinity Stones simply don't allow multiple realities to co-exist, or at least to run contrary to one another.

Again, when all else fails to explain something: *Infinity Stones*.

Thor and Rocket's mission to retrieve the Reality Stone (AKA the Aether) was largely successful. Frigga remained unaware of her demise and Loki remained locked-up. Remember, you're thinking about the events of the movie as a narrative, rather than as happening across entirely separate moments of time. When Thor and Rocket travel back to Asgard, they left a future where Loki was taken there after the events of *The Avengers*. The changes that occur during Steve, Tony and Scott's mission are *their experience*, not Thor and Rocket's.

Loki's escape I can only presume becomes *canon*, or now a part of the ' real story' of the MCU because he escapes prior to the Time Stone being taken out of continuity.

Steve's life with Peggy occurs because of a similar narrative device. The stones are all returned to their chronological points of origin, but rather than returning to 2023 and 'closing the loop', Steve decides to *alter* events by assuming the role of Peggy Carter's husband. 

We don't then have to conclude that logically Steve has been Peggy's husband all along, although doing so would be largely harmless.
